subject: geography_ib
source: Podstawa programowa kształcenia ogólnego dla liceum i technikum, geografia, zakres podstawowy (Dz.U. 2018 poz. 467), działy I–V (klasa 1); pojęcia tylko z IB DP Geography core oznaczone "IB core"

items.question: On a map at the scale 1:50 000, how much real distance does 1 cm represent?
items.explanation: Divide the scale denominator by 100 000 to get kilometres per centimetre: 50 000 cm = 500 m = 0.5 km.

items.question: On a 1:25 000 map two towns are 8 cm apart. What is the real distance?
Which map has the larger scale: 1:10 000 or 1:1 000 000?
items.explanation: A larger scale means a smaller denominator and more detail on a smaller area.

items.text: A map scale written as a fraction, e.g. 1:100 000, is called a {{numerical/representative fraction/ratio}} scale.
items.hint: as opposed to a linear (bar) scale
items.explanation: The other common forms are the linear (bar) scale and the verbal scale (1 cm to 1 km).

items.text: Lines on a map joining points of equal elevation above sea level are called {{contour lines/contours/isohypses}}.
items.explanation: Closely spaced contours mean a steep slope; widely spaced contours mean gentle terrain.

items.question: What is the general name for a line on a map joining points with the same value of a phenomenon (e.g. temperature, pressure)?
items.explanation: Isotherms join equal temperatures, isobars equal pressure, isohyets equal rainfall.

items.question: Which cartographic method shows the value of a phenomenon per administrative unit with shading or colour intensity?
items.explanation: Choropleth maps are typical for population density or GDP per capita by country or region.

items.question: Which map method uses symbols or circles scaled in size to show quantities, e.g. city populations?
items.explanation: The size of the symbol is proportional to the value it represents.

items.question: What is the name of a map that shows the shape of the land, roads, rivers and buildings at a large scale?
items.explanation: Topographic maps are general-purpose maps; thematic maps show one phenomenon.

items.text: A map that presents one chosen phenomenon, e.g. climate zones or population density, is a {{thematic}} map.
items.explanation: Thematic maps use methods such as choropleths, isolines and symbols.

items.question: What is the name of the method of transferring the curved surface of the Earth onto a flat map?
items.explanation: Every projection distorts something: area, shape, distance or direction.

items.question: Which classic cylindrical projection keeps shapes and angles but greatly enlarges areas near the poles (Greenland looks as big as Africa)?
items.explanation: Mercator is conformal, so it is used for navigation, but it is not equal-area.

items.question: What does the abbreviation GIS stand for?
items.explanation: GIS stores, analyses and displays spatial data in layers such as roads, land use and elevation.

items.question: What does the abbreviation GPS stand for?
items.explanation: A GPS receiver calculates its latitude and longitude from signals of at least four satellites.

items.question: What is the general term for obtaining information about the Earth's surface from satellites or aircraft without direct contact?
items.explanation: Satellite images are used to monitor deforestation, floods, urban growth and weather.

items.question: Which planet of the Solar System is third from the Sun?
items.explanation: The order is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

items.question: How many planets does the Solar System have?
items.explanation: Pluto has been classified as a dwarf planet since 2006.

items.text: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are called the {{terrestrial/rocky/inner}} planets, while Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are gas giants.
items.explanation: The rocky planets are small and dense; the giants are large and made mostly of gas and ice.

items.question: What is the name of a system of billions of stars held together by gravity, such as the Milky Way?
items.explanation: The Solar System lies in one of the spiral arms of the Milky Way galaxy.

items.question: What is the name of the Earth's movement around its own axis?
items.explanation: One rotation takes about 24 hours and causes day and night.

items.question: What is the name of the Earth's movement around the Sun?
items.explanation: One revolution takes about 365.25 days; the extra quarter day is why we have leap years.

items.question: By how many degrees is the Earth's axis tilted from the perpendicular to its orbital plane?
items.explanation: The axial tilt, not the distance from the Sun, is the cause of the seasons.

items.question: Name the apparent force caused by the Earth's rotation that deflects moving air and water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.
items.explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere the deflection is to the left; it shapes wind belts and ocean gyres.

items.text: On the day of the {{solstice}} (around 21 June) the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer and the Northern Hemisphere has its longest day.
items.explanation: At the equinoxes (around 21 March and 23 September) the Sun is overhead at the equator and day equals night everywhere.

items.question: At what latitude is the Sun directly overhead at noon on the equinoxes?
items.explanation: On the equinoxes day and night last 12 hours at every latitude.

items.question: By how many degrees of longitude does the Earth rotate in one hour?
items.explanation: 360 degrees / 24 hours = 15 degrees per hour, which is the width of one time zone.

items.question: It is 12:00 UTC in London (0 degrees). What is the solar time at 30 degrees E?
items.explanation: Every 15 degrees eastward adds one hour: 30 degrees E = +2 hours.

items.question: Along which meridian does the International Date Line approximately run?
items.explanation: Crossing it westward you add a day; crossing it eastward you subtract a day.

items.question: Which gas makes up about 78% of dry air?
items.explanation: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and about 1% argon and trace gases, including 0.04% CO2.

items.question: What percentage of dry air is oxygen?
items.explanation: Oxygen is the second most abundant gas after nitrogen.

items.question: In which layer of the atmosphere does almost all weather occur?
items.explanation: The troposphere extends to about 8-18 km and contains most water vapour; temperature falls with height in it.

items.question: Which layer of the atmosphere contains the ozone layer?
items.explanation: Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs most of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation.

items.question: By roughly how many degrees Celsius does the air temperature fall per 100 m of altitude in the troposphere?
items.explanation: This average lapse rate is about 6 degrees C per 1000 m.

items.question: What is the normal atmospheric pressure at sea level in hectopascals?
items.explanation: Pressure decreases with altitude because there is less air above.

items.text: The most important climate-forming factor is {{latitude}}, because it determines the angle at which the Sun's rays reach the surface.
items.explanation: Other factors: altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, relief and prevailing winds.

items.question: What is the name of the effect in which the sea moderates the climate of nearby land (cooler summers, milder winters)?
items.explanation: Water heats and cools more slowly than land, which reduces the annual temperature range near coasts.

items.text: The low-pressure belt of rising air around the equator is called the {{Intertropical Convergence Zone/ITCZ/equatorial low}}.
items.explanation: Rising warm, moist air here produces daily convectional rainfall in the equatorial zone.

items.text: Subtropical high-pressure belts at about {{30}} degrees latitude are the location of most of the world's hot deserts.
items.hint: between the equator and the mid-latitudes
items.explanation: Sinking dry air (the descending limb of the Hadley cell) suppresses cloud and rain.

items.question: Which winds blow from the subtropical highs towards the equator?
items.explanation: They blow from the north-east in the Northern Hemisphere and from the south-east in the Southern Hemisphere.

items.question: Which winds dominate the mid-latitudes (e.g. over Poland and western Europe)?
items.explanation: They bring moist Atlantic air masses and changeable weather to Europe.

items.question: What is the name of the seasonal wind system in South Asia that brings heavy summer rain?
items.explanation: In summer the wind blows from the ocean onto the land; in winter it reverses and is dry.

items.text: The atmospheric circulation cell between the equator and about 30 degrees latitude is the {{Hadley}} cell.
items.explanation: The other cells are the Ferrel cell (30-60 degrees) and the polar cell (60-90 degrees).

items.question: Which type of rainfall is caused by moist air being forced to rise over a mountain barrier?
items.explanation: The leeward side of the mountains receives little rain and is called the rain shadow.

items.question: Which type of rainfall results from the heating of the ground and the rapid rising of warm air?
items.explanation: Typical of the equatorial zone and of hot summer afternoons in the mid-latitudes.

items.question: Which type of rainfall occurs when warm air is lifted over a mass of cold air along a front?
items.explanation: Most rain in Poland falls from fronts of mid-latitude depressions.

items.question: Which pressure system in the Northern Hemisphere has winds blowing clockwise outwards and brings settled, dry weather?
items.explanation: In a depression (low) the air rises and the winds blow anticlockwise inwards, bringing cloud and rain.

items.question: What is the name of a map showing the weather at a given moment with isobars, fronts and station data?
items.explanation: Meteorologists use synoptic charts to describe the current weather and forecast its changes.

items.text: Lines on a synoptic map joining points of equal atmospheric pressure are called {{isobars}}.
items.explanation: Closely spaced isobars mean a strong pressure gradient and strong winds.

items.question: What is the name of the boundary between two air masses of different temperature?
items.explanation: A warm front brings prolonged light rain; a cold front brings short, heavy showers.

items.text: Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a given moment and place, while {{climate}} is the average pattern of weather in a region over about 30 years.
items.explanation: Weather changes from hour to hour; climate describes typical conditions, e.g. the climate of Poland.

items.question: What climate type has Poland, with mild winters in the west and colder, more continental winters in the east?
items.explanation: Poland lies between the maritime climate of western Europe and the continental climate of eastern Europe.

items.question: Which climate zone has high temperatures all year and rainfall almost every day?
items.explanation: Average monthly temperatures stay around 25-28 degrees C and annual rainfall exceeds 2000 mm.

items.text: The climate zone with the greatest annual temperature range and cold winters, typical of Siberia and inland Canada, is the {{continental}} type of the temperate zone.
items.explanation: Continental climates have hot summers, very cold winters and relatively low rainfall.

items.text: The warming of the lower atmosphere by gases such as CO2, methane and water vapour that absorb outgoing long-wave radiation is called the {{greenhouse effect}}.
items.explanation: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth habitable; its enhancement by human emissions drives current global warming.

items.question: Roughly what percentage of the Earth's water is salt water in the oceans?
items.explanation: Only about 3% is fresh water, and most of that is locked in ice sheets and glaciers.

items.question: Where is most of the Earth's fresh water stored?
items.explanation: About two-thirds of fresh water is ice; most of the rest is groundwater, and rivers and lakes hold less than 1%.

items.question: What is the name of the continuous movement of water between oceans, atmosphere and land through evaporation, condensation and precipitation?
items.explanation: Solar energy drives evaporation; gravity returns water to the sea as runoff.

items.question: What is the average salinity of ocean water in per mille?
items.explanation: Salinity is higher in the subtropics (strong evaporation) and lower near the poles and river mouths.

items.question: What is the approximate salinity of the Baltic Sea?
items.explanation: The Baltic is brackish because of heavy river inflow and limited exchange with the North Sea.

items.text: The warm ocean current that gives western Europe milder winters than other places at the same latitude is the {{Gulf Stream/North Atlantic Drift}}.
items.hint: flows from the Gulf of Mexico
items.explanation: Warm currents flow from the tropics towards the poles along the eastern coasts of continents.

items.text: The cold current off the coast of Peru and Chile that cools the climate and causes the Atacama Desert is the {{Humboldt/Peru}} Current.
items.explanation: Cold currents reduce evaporation and rainfall, producing coastal deserts; upwelling makes them rich fishing grounds.

items.question: What is the main driving force of surface ocean currents?
items.explanation: Winds push the surface water, the Coriolis force deflects it, and continents turn the flow into large gyres.

items.question: What is the name of the area of land drained by a river and its tributaries?
items.explanation: Drainage basins are separated from each other by watersheds (drainage divides).

items.text: An area of land from which no river reaches the ocean (e.g. much of Central Asia with the Aral Sea) is a region of {{inland/endorheic}} drainage.
items.hint: the opposite of draining to the sea
items.explanation: Rivers there end in inland lakes, salt pans or disappear by evaporation.

items.question: What is the name of the flat area beside a river that is covered with water during floods?
items.explanation: Floodplains are fertile but risky places for settlement.

items.question: What is the largest hot desert region where there are no permanent rivers except the Nile?
items.explanation: The Nile is an allochthonous river: it gets its water from wetter areas far upstream.

items.text: A glacier forms when, over many years, more snow accumulates than melts and it is compacted into {{firn}} and then glacial ice.
items.explanation: The boundary above which snow survives the summer is called the snow line.

items.question: Which two regions hold the world's only ice sheets (continental glaciers)?
items.explanation: Mountain (alpine) glaciers occur on all continents, e.g. in the Alps, Himalayas and Andes.

items.question: What are the three main layers of the Earth's interior?
accept: the crust, the mantle and the core
items.explanation: The core is divided into a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.

items.question: What is the name of the rigid outer shell of the Earth made of the crust and the uppermost mantle, broken into plates?
items.explanation: Below it lies the asthenosphere, a partly molten layer on which the plates move.

items.text: Tectonic plates move because of {{convection currents}} in the mantle.
items.hint: hot material rises, cool material sinks
items.explanation: Heat from the core drives slow circulation of the mantle, which drags the plates along.

items.question: Which type of crust is thinner and denser: oceanic or continental?
items.explanation: Oceanic crust is 5-10 km of basalt; continental crust is 30-70 km of lighter granitic rock.

items.question: What type of plate boundary is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where plates move apart?
items.explanation: Magma rises to fill the gap and forms new oceanic crust (sea-floor spreading).

items.question: What type of plate boundary is the San Andreas Fault, where plates slide past each other?
items.explanation: No crust is created or destroyed, but friction causes strong earthquakes.

items.text: At a convergent boundary where an oceanic plate sinks under another plate, a deep ocean {{trench}} and a line of volcanoes form.
items.hint: the deepest parts of the ocean
items.explanation: The sinking of a plate into the mantle is called subduction; the Mariana Trench is an example.

items.question: Which mountain range formed from the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates?
items.explanation: Collision of two continental plates folds the crust upwards; the Himalayas are still rising.

items.question: What is the name of the process of mountain building by folding and faulting of the crust?
items.explanation: The Alps, Himalayas and Andes were formed in the Alpine orogeny.

items.question: What is the name of the point inside the Earth where an earthquake originates?
items.explanation: The point on the surface directly above the focus is the epicentre, where shaking is usually strongest.

items.question: What is the name of the point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus of an earthquake?
items.explanation: Seismic waves spread out from the epicentre.

items.question: Which scale measures the magnitude (energy) of an earthquake with a logarithmic scale?
items.explanation: Each whole step on the scale means about 32 times more energy released.

items.text: The zone around the Pacific Ocean with most of the world's active volcanoes and earthquakes is called the {{Ring of Fire/Pacific Ring of Fire}}.
items.explanation: It follows the subduction zones around the edges of the Pacific plate.

items.question: What is the name of the slow uplift or subsidence of large areas of the crust without folding?
items.explanation: Scandinavia is still rising after the weight of the ice sheet was removed.

items.text: Molten rock below the Earth's surface is called {{magma}}; once it erupts onto the surface it is called lava.
items.explanation: Magma that cools slowly underground forms intrusive rocks such as granite (plutonism).

items.question: What is the name of the large depression formed when a volcano's summit collapses after a huge eruption?
items.explanation: Calderas may fill with water, e.g. Crater Lake in the USA.

items.question: What is the breakdown of rock in place by frost, temperature changes, water or organisms called?
items.explanation: Unlike erosion, weathering does not involve transport of the material.

items.question: What type of weathering is the shattering of rock by water freezing and expanding in cracks?
items.explanation: It is a type of physical (mechanical) weathering, common in high mountains and cold climates.

items.question: What type of weathering is the dissolving of limestone by rainwater containing carbon dioxide?
items.explanation: This process (carbonation) creates karst landforms such as caves and sinkholes.

items.question: Name the three stages of the work of external (exogenic) forces on the Earth's surface.
items.explanation: Rivers, wind, glaciers and the sea all erode, carry and deposit material.

items.question: What landform is created where a river deposits sediment at its mouth, forming new land with many channels?
items.explanation: The Nile and Mississippi deltas are classic examples; an estuary forms instead where tides remove the sediment.

items.question: What is the name of a bowl-shaped hollow in the mountains eroded by a glacier, often holding a lake?
items.explanation: Glaciers also carve U-shaped valleys, while rivers cut V-shaped valleys.

items.question: What is the name of a hill of sand built up by the wind in a desert or on a coast?
items.explanation: Wind also polishes rocks (corrasion) and sweeps away fine material (deflation).

items.question: What is the name of the group of rocks formed from the cooling of magma or lava, such as granite and basalt?
items.explanation: The other two groups are sedimentary rocks (limestone, sandstone) and metamorphic rocks (marble, gneiss).

items.question: What is the name of the number of live births per 1000 people per year?
items.explanation: IB Geography core, Unit 1 Changing population; the crude death rate is the number of deaths per 1000 people per year.

items.question: In the Demographic Transition Model, in which stage are both birth and death rates high and the population grows slowly?
items.explanation: Stage 2: death rate falls, rapid growth; stage 3: birth rate falls; stage 4: both low; stage 5: birth rate below death rate.

items.text: The {{dependency ratio}} compares the number of people aged 0-14 and over 65 with the working-age population aged 15-64.
items.explanation: A high ratio puts pressure on health care, pensions and education.

items.question: What is the name of the rise in global sea level caused by water expanding as it warms, in addition to melting ice?
items.explanation: IB Geography core, Unit 3 Global climate: sea-level rise threatens low-lying islands and deltas.

items.text: Actions that reduce greenhouse gas emissions, such as switching to renewable energy, are called climate change {{mitigation}}, while coping with its effects, e.g. building sea walls, is adaptation.
items.explanation: Mitigation targets the cause; adaptation targets the consequences.

items.text: The amount of greenhouse gases emitted by a person, product or country, expressed in tonnes of CO2 equivalent, is its carbon {{footprint}}.
items.explanation: Carbon footprints are much higher in high-income countries than in low-income ones.
